_about: Analyst-maintained list of code-signing certificates known to have been STOLEN or ABUSED by malware. tools/authenticode.py correlates a sample's signer against this list. This ships as a STARTER list — extend it from your own threat intel (VT, vendor reports, CISA advisories). It is intentionally small and conservative: better to under-match than to fabricate a thumbprint.

_schema.name: human label for the abused cert / incident
_schema.thumbprint_sha1: leaf cert SHA-1 fingerprint (hex). A match here is a HARD hit -> flag abused_cert (High).
_schema.thumbprint_sha256: leaf cert SHA-256 fingerprint (hex). HARD hit.
_schema.serial: cert serial number (decimal string, as signify renders it). HARD hit.
_schema.signer_name: substring of the signer/issuer CN. A match here is a SOFT hit -> flag abused_cert_suspected (Investigate), because names are not unique and a legit re-issued cert can share a name. Add the real thumbprint to upgrade it to a hard match.
_schema.reference: URL / advisory ID documenting the abuse

_usage: To turn a SOFT name match into a HARD match, obtain the actual stolen cert's SHA-1/SHA-256 thumbprint from the vendor report or VT and add it to the entry. Hard matches assert abuse; soft matches only flag it for analyst review.

certs.name: Realtek Semiconductor Corp (Stuxnet, 2010)
certs.note: Code-signing cert stolen and used to sign Stuxnet drivers. Realtek revoked it. Soft/name match only here — supply the actual thumbprint from your TI to make it a hard hit. A modern legit Realtek-signed driver will NOT carry the revoked serial, so verify before trusting a name match.

certs.name: JMicron Technology Corp (Stuxnet, 2010)
certs.note: Second stolen cert used by Stuxnet after the Realtek cert was revoked. Name match is Investigate-grade only.
